turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.problem: Tell me about a project you really owned
card.heard: pick the project, who used it, my responsibility
card.say: The AI trip planner at KKday is the one I'd pick. I was the technical lead for a five-person team. Travelers used it in our Android app. Planning a trip by hand was slow: work out the budget, search products one by one, then put the plan together. My responsibility started at the technical plan and the agent design.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer's follow-up on this project.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names a real project (AI trip planner at KKday), its users (travelers in the Android app), the problem (slow manual trip planning), and the candidate's scope (technical lead, technical plan and agent design), with no invented details.
judge.criterion: SAY introduces one real Android project from the candidate's background with its users, the problem and the candidate's own scope; no invented employers, titles or numbers.

turns.name: P1-dyn
turns.question: On the AI trip planner at KKday, you said your responsibility started at the technical plan and agent design — which exact pieces did you build yourself versus delegate to the five-person team?

card.problem: Tell me about a project you really owned
card.heard: which pieces I built myself versus delegated
card.say: I built the agent design and the core backend myself. I also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan. The other four people worked on the app screens, the product side and testing. I set the response format with the app team, but they built the screens.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer's follow-up on this project.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies what the candidate personally built (agent design, core backend, Android streaming code) versus delegated (screens, product side, testing), which follows from the earlier statement that responsibility started at technical plan and agent design, adds concrete detail rather than repeating, stays consistent with the five-person team and Android app context, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-change
turns.question: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?

card.problem: Walk through one change I personally made, from user action through UI, data or network
card.adopted: SSE stream from the backend, parsed on Android and shown day by day
card.heard: pick one change I personally made, walk from user action through UI, data or network
card.say: The change I made myself is the Android side of the streamed plan. The user enters a destination, a budget and the number of days. The app sends that to our backend and opens an SSE connection. Each day card arrives as its own event, so the app parses it and shows Day 1 while the rest is still being made. I wrote that reading and parsing code, and the format it expects.
card.then: Next: where that parsing runs, and what happens when the stream breaks.

more: The user action is entering a destination, a budget and the number of days. The app sends that to our backend and opens an SSE connection. If the connection drops mid-stream, the client reconnects with the last received day index so already-shown cards aren't duplicated.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer traces a user action (entering destination, budget, days) through UI, network (SSE connection), and parsing/state (day cards arriving as events, showing Day 1 while rest streams), and states the candidate wrote the reading/parsing code and the format it expects. It separates own work (Android streamed-plan parsing) from the team's (app team built screens), and contains no invented numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY traces one user action through concrete layers (UI, state, data or network) and says which logic the candidate changed; separates own work from the team's; no invented numbers.

turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Hardest bug to reproduce in the streamed plan, what I suspected and what proved me wrong
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, what I suspected, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest one was a day card that sometimes showed twice. I first suspected the backend was sending the same event twice. But the logs showed the client reconnected and asked for the last day index, and the server sent that day again. So the fix was on my side: I skip any day index I already have. I proved it by cutting the network in the middle of a stream and checking the cards.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a clear timeline — first suspicion (backend sending duplicate events), evidence that overturned it (logs showing client reconnect and server resending the last day), and root cause (client-side dedup needed), with the repro (cutting the network mid-stream) as verification; observation (logs) is distinguished from conclusion (fix on my side).
judge.criterion: SAY gives a timeline: first suspicion, the evidence (log, experiment or repro) that overturned it, and the root cause, distinguishing observation from conclusion.

turns.name: P2-dyn
turns.question: You said you proved it by cutting the network mid-stream — how did you confirm the duplicate was actually gone rather than just not seeing it that time?

card.problem: Hardest bug to reproduce in the streamed plan, what I suspected and what proved me wrong
card.heard: how did you confirm the duplicate was gone, not just not seen that time
card.say: I didn't trust one lucky run. I made the test repeatable. I added a debug switch that drops the connection after Day 1, every time. Then I ran it many times and checked the logs. Each day index appeared once, and the reconnect asked for the right index.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds on the earlier mid-stream test by making it repeatable with a debug switch, adds specifics (drops after Day 1, repeated runs, logs showing each index once and correct reconnect index), stays consistent with the SSE/day-index story and the candidate's Android/backend role, is technically sound, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-alt
turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Hardest bug to reproduce in the streamed plan, what I suspected and what proved me wrong
card.heard: other options, why not them, how I knew it worked after release
card.say: There were two other options. First, the server could keep the full plan and resend it from the start. That wastes bandwidth and makes the user wait again. Second, the client could ask for the whole plan again after a drop. That's slower and costs more.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names two real alternatives (server resends full plan; client re-requests whole plan) and the constraints that ruled them out (bandwidth/wait; slower and costlier), and it gives the source of the result (repeatable test with a debug switch dropping the connection after Day 1, run many times with logs checked) — though it does not explicitly state the limits of that evidence, the criterion's examples are covered and nothing stated is wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY names a real alternative and the constraint that ruled it out, and the source of the result (metric, test, ticket or feedback) with its limits.

turns.name: P3-risk
turns.question: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?

card.problem: Hardest bug to reproduce in the streamed plan, what I suspected and what proved me wrong
card.heard: a time a delivery risk or likely delay caused disagreement
card.say: At KKday, we were close to a release, and I found a broken back button on some old pages. I hadn't checked every page yet. I told the project manager the same day. I gave two options: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and test fast. He chose to move my change.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a concrete KKday case with when (same day, close to release), whom (project manager), two options, who decided (the PM chose to move the change), and the candidate's own action (found the broken back button, raised it), with no wrong details.
judge.criterion: SAY describes one concrete case: when and whom the candidate told, the options offered, who had the decision, and what the candidate personally did; attributes the case to the right company.

turns.name: P3-dyn
turns.question: You said the PM chose to move your change — what risk were you willing to accept before that release, and who watched the data afterwards? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?

card.problem: A delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, the options, who decided, what I finished
card.heard: what risk I accepted, who watched the data, what signal would pause or roll back
card.say: The risk I accepted was the pages I hadn't checked yet. I kept testing them while the rest of the release went out. For that release, the signal was simple: any crash or broken back button on the old pages. If we saw that, I'd pause the rollout and fix it first. After release, I watched the crash reports in Bugly and the support tickets for that flow.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names a specific accepted risk (untested old pages), a concrete rollback signal (crash or broken back button), and who watched data (the candidate via Bugly crash reports and support tickets), consistent with the earlier PM decision and without inventing employers, titles, metrics, or wallet rules.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W1-scope
turns.question: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.heard: switch to design exercise — mobile wallet, clarify requirements, define MVP path
card.say: Good evening. Before I design anything, let me confirm the scope. For the MVP, I'd pick one path: person-to-person payment. A user picks a contact, enters an amount, confirms on a native screen, and sees the result. Does that match what you want?
card.then: Next, I'd go into the data model and how a transfer is made safe.

more: I'd also keep top-ups and merchant payments out of the MVP.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer proposes one MVP path (person-to-person payment to a contact) and asks a scope-confirming question ("Does that match what you want?"), covering the MVP-path example; it says nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY asks clarifying questions about scope (stored balance vs external rail, currency, offline behaviour, authority of the ledger) and proposes one MVP path such as send money to a contact.

turns.name: W2-design
turns.question: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["MVP is person-to-person payment: pick a contact, enter an amount, confirm on a native screen, see the result", "Closed wallet with a stored balance topped up from a bank card; server is the source of truth for money", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: requirements given, draw the flowchart
card.say: Got it. The local store only caches reads.
card.type: draw@wallet design: flowchart TD ⏎     A[Android app: screens, transfer ID] -->|submit transfer| B[Wallet server: ledger, limits] ⏎     A -->|cached reads| C[Local storage: last known balance and history] ⏎     B -->|confirmed balance and history| A ⏎     B --> D[(Ledger: append-only entries)]
card.then: Next, I'd walk through one transfer and where it can fail.

more: The board already shows the three parts and what each one owns. The app owns the screens and the transfer ID. The server owns the ledger and the limits. Local storage only holds the last known balance and history for offline reads. One thing to add: the server checks and moves the money in one database transaction.

diagram.type: draw@wallet design: flowchart TD ⏎     A[Android app: screens, transfer ID] -->|

judge.detail: FAIL: The TYPE flowchart only shows a single "Android app" node, not the required UI, ViewModel, repository, and local database layers, and SAY does not state that the server ledger is the authority.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of the Android client (UI, ViewModel, repository, local database), the server and its ledger; SAY says what each part owns and that the server ledger is the authority.

turns.name: W2-seq
turns.question: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["MVP is person-to-person payment: pick a contact, enter an amount, confirm on a native screen, see the result", "Closed wallet with a stored balance topped up from a bank card; server is the source of truth for money", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: draw the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars
card.say: Okay, I'll draw the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars. The app sends the transfer ID and the amount, 8000 cents, after the user confirms. The server checks A's balance and writes both ledger entries in one transaction. Then it returns the transfer status, and the app shows the result screen from that record.
card.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as App (A) ⏎     participant S as Wallet server ⏎     participant L as Ledger ⏎     A->>S: confirm: transfer ID, B, 8000 cents ⏎     S->>L: one transaction: debit A, credit B ⏎     L-->>S: new balances ⏎     S-->>A: transfer status ⏎     A->>A: show result screen
card.then: Next, I'd cover the failure cases: a timeout, a retry with the same ID, and a dropped connection.

more: The sequence is on the board now. One thing I'd add: the app shows success only from the server's transfer record, never from a local guess. And the server binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry, so chat text can never authorize a payment.

diagram.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as App (A) ⏎     part

judge.detail: FAIL: The SAY does not state the final balances (A 20 dollars, B 80) or the result states, and the diagram's response/result coverage is thin.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid sequenceDiagram covering confirm, submit with a client transfer ID, an atomic server debit and credit, the response and the result; SAY covers amounts in cents and the final balances (A 20 dollars, B 80) and the result states.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the app sends the transfer ID and 8000 cents after the user confirms — what exactly is stored locally before that request goes out, and how does the result screen behave while it's waiting?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["MVP is person-to-person payment: pick a contact, enter an amount, confirm on a native screen, see the result", "Closed wallet with a stored balance topped up from a bank card; server is the source of truth for money", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: what is stored locally before the request, and the result screen while waiting
card.say: Before the request, I store the transfer ID, the amount in cents, the recipient and the status "sending". The result screen opens right away in a pending state. It shows the amount and the recipient, and a clear "sending" label, not a spinner alone. If the response is lost, it keeps that state and queries the same transfer ID. It only shows success or failure from the server's record.
card.then: Next, what the server does when the same transfer ID arrives twice.

more: The pending record lives in the local database, so it survives process death. When the app comes back, it reads that record and shows the same pending state. The screen never guesses the result.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies local storage of transfer ID, amount, recipient, and "sending" status, describes the result screen's pending state with amount/recipient and a clear label, and handles lost responses by querying the same transfer ID — all consistent with the earlier sequence diagram and the rule that success comes only from the server's record, with no invented details.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W3-change1
turns.question: Your sequence ends with "S-->>A: transfer status" and the app showing the result, which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before A reopens — what changes in your flow? Please update your sequence diagram.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["MVP is person-to-person payment: pick a contact, enter an amount, confirm on a native screen, see the result", "Closed wallet with a stored balance topped up from a bank card; server is the source of truth for money", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: server commits, response lost, process killed before A reopens
card.say: Right, so the response never reaches the app. The app already saved the pending record before sending, so after the process is killed it reopens and reads that record. It shows "sending" again, not success and not failure. Then it queries the server with the same transfer ID and shows whatever status comes back.
card.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as App (A) ⏎     participant S as Wallet server ⏎     participant L as Ledger ⏎     A->>S: confirm: transfer ID, B, 8000 cents ⏎     S->>L: one transaction: debit A, credit B ⏎     L-->>S: new balances ⏎     Note over A: response lost, process killed ⏎     A->>A: reopen: read pending record ⏎     A->>S: query: same transfer ID ⏎     S-->>A: original status ⏎     A->>A: show result from record
card.then: Next, what the server does when the same transfer ID arrives twice.

more: The board now shows that case. The app reopens, reads the pending record, and asks the server with the same transfer ID. The server would need to answer with the original status, not start a new transfer. So the user sees the real result, even after a restart.

diagram.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as App (A) ⏎     part

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the outcome as unknown ("sending," not success/failure), persists the pending record with the transfer ID before sending, reopens and queries the server with the same transfer ID, and states the server returns the original status rather than starting a new transfer — covering the key points with nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY and TYPE treat the outcome as unknown (not failed), persist the transfer intent ID before sending, query the server by account and that ID after restart, and replay the same intent only if the server's idempotency contract allows; the server returns the original transfer's status for a repeat of the same ID; never a new ID; ledger has one transfer.

turns.name: W3-dyn
turns.question: You said the server answers with the original status for the same transfer ID — what does the app show if that lookup comes back not found?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["MVP is person-to-person payment: pick a contact, enter an amount, confirm on a native screen, see the result", "Closed wallet with a stored balance topped up from a bank card; server is the source of truth for money", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: what does the app show if the lookup comes back not found
card.say: Not found means the server has no record of that transfer ID. So the money never moved, and I'd show "not sent" with a retry button. The app would never show success from a missing record. I'd also log it, because a missing record after a confirm is a real problem.
card.then: Next, what the server does when the same transfer ID arrives twice.

more: I'd keep the pending record until the user acts, and on retry I'd resend the same transfer ID rather than a new one, so a slow first request can't move the money twice.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer correctly treats "not found" as no server record (so no money moved), shows "not sent" with retry rather than success, and adds specifics (logging, keeping the pending record, resending the same transfer ID) that are consistent with the earlier idempotency design and invent no new rules or credentials.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W4-concurrency
turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["MVP is person-to-person payment: pick a contact, enter an amount, confirm on a native screen, see the result", "Closed wallet with a stored balance topped up from a bank card; server is the source of truth for money", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: two phones, two 80 dollar transfers at the same time
card.say: Only one can succeed. A has 100 dollars, so the first one to reach the server takes 80 and leaves 20. The second one fails the balance check, because 20 is less than 80. The server decides this inside one transaction with a row lock on A's account, so both requests can't read 100 at the same time. Each phone shows the result from its own transfer record: one success, one "not enough balance".
card.then: Next, what the server does when the same transfer ID arrives twice.

more: The second phone shows a clear failure, not a pending state, and A's balance stays at 20 dollars. The first phone shows success with the new balance. Both phones then read the server's record, so they agree.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the two transfers as separate intents, has the server decide inside one transaction with a row lock on A's account, shows one success and one insufficient-balance failure, and leaves A at 20 dollars.
judge.criterion: SAY treats them as two intents with separate IDs, checks and debits the balance in one transaction (row lock or conditional update), one succeeds and one fails for insufficient funds, A ends at 20 dollars.

turns.name: W5-account
turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.problem: Hardest bug to reproduce in the streamed plan, what I suspected and what proved me wrong
card.heard: account switched to C, then A's old response arrives
card.say: The old response belongs to account A, so it must never touch C's screen. I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation. When the response comes back, I compare that tag with the current session. If it doesn't match, I drop it. The result for A is already saved on the server, so A sees it from its own record after signing in again.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer tags requests/callbacks with account and session generation, drops stale responses on mismatch, prevents C from seeing A's data, and notes A's committed transfer is recovered from A's own record after signing in again.
judge.criterion: SAY scopes cache writes and UI to account and session, drops callbacks from a stale session, C never sees A's data, and A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after A signs in again.

turns.name: W6-change2
turns.question: You said the result screen opens right away in a pending state — now the flow starts from a chat message "pay Alex for last night's dinner" with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, and the chat stream disconnects after confirm. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see? Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.

card.problem: Chat message entry with two Alex contacts, no reliable amount, and the chat stream dropping after confirm
card.adopted: Chat message is only an input; the app asks for the missing recipient and amount, then the user confirms on a native screen before anything is sent
card.constraints: ["Entry starts from a chat message: pay Alex for last night\'s dinner", "Two contacts are named Alex, so the recipient is ambiguous", "There is no reliable amount in the chat", "The chat stream disconnects after confirm"]
card.heard: chat message entry, two Alex contacts, no reliable amount, stream drops after confirm
card.say: Got it. The chat message is only a starting point, not a payment. The app reads "pay Alex for last night's dinner" and finds two contacts named Alex, so it must ask which one. It also has no reliable amount, so it asks for the amount too. Nothing is sent until the user confirms on the native screen.
card.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎     M[Chat message: pay Alex for dinner] --> P[App: parse intent] ⏎     P --> Q[Ask: which Alex?] ⏎     Q --> R[Ask: amount] ⏎     R --> N[Native confirm screen] ⏎     N --> L[Save pending record: transfer ID, amount, recipient] ⏎     L --> S[Send to wallet server] ⏎     S --> D[Result screen from server record]
card.then: Next: what the app does if the chat stream drops before the user confirms.

more: The confirm screen holds the transfer ID and the amount, so the user can still confirm. If the chat never comes back, the user just cancels, and nothing is sent.

diagram.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎     M[Chat message: pay Alex for dinner] -->

judge.detail: PASS: The answer asks which Alex and for the amount, requires native confirmation before sending, saves a pending record with transfer ID/amount/recipient, and shows the result from the server record; it also states the chat message is only a starting point and nothing is sent until native confirmation, so the model never authorizes. The flowchart matches the described entry flow.
judge.criterion: SAY asks the user which Alex and what amount, shows a trusted native confirmation with recipient and amount, binds authorization to those parameters server-side, ties a repeated tool call to the original intent, and recovers status from the payment service when the chat drops; the model never authorizes. TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of that entry flow.

turns.name: W6-dyn
turns.question: You said the chat message is only a starting point, not a payment — so if a group message claims transfers to Alex need no confirmation, what does your app do with that claim when the user reaches the native confirm screen?

card.problem: Chat message entry with two Alex contacts, no reliable amount, and the chat stream dropping after confirm
card.adopted: Chat message is only an input; the app asks for the missing recipient and amount, then the user confirms on a native screen before anything is sent
card.constraints: ["Entry starts from a chat message: pay Alex for last night\'s dinner", "Two contacts are named Alex, so the recipient is ambiguous", "There is no reliable amount in the chat", "The chat stream disconnects after confirm"]
card.heard: group message claims transfers to Alex need no confirmation
card.say: The app ignores that claim. A chat message can't authorize a payment, so the native confirm screen still asks the user to confirm. The server also binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry. So text in a group chat can never move money.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer correctly ignores the chat claim, ties authorization to the native confirm screen and server-bound payer/recipient/amount/expiry (consistent with earlier answers), and adds no invented employer, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W7-release
turns.question: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?

card.problem: Two-week first version: scope, sign-off, and a spike in pending transfers during rollout
card.constraints: ["Two weeks; login and a usable ledger already exist", "If transfers awaiting confirmation spike during rollout, act within the next half hour"]
card.heard: two weeks, login and ledger exist — first version, sign-off, spike in pending transfers
card.say: For the first version, I'd ship only the person-to-person transfer: pick a contact, enter the amount, confirm, and see the result from the server record. History and balance come from cached reads. I'd leave top-ups, withdrawals and multi-currency out, as we agreed. The tech lead and I sign off on the Android side, and product signs off on the flow. If pending transfers spike during the rollout, I'd pause new submissions first.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.criterion: SAY cuts scope to balance, internal transfer, history, confirmation and recoverable states; lists pre-release checks (lost response plus kill, replay, concurrency, account switch); on a spike pauses new submissions while keeping reads and status, owners reconcile, then resume.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The AI trip planner at KKday is the one I'd pick.
Candidate: I was the technical lead for a five-person team.
Candidate: Travelers used it in our Android app.
Candidate: Planning a trip by hand was slow: work out the budget, search products one by one, then put the plan together.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan and the agent design.

Interviewer: On the AI trip planner at KKday, you said your responsibility started at the technical plan and agent design — which exact pieces did you build yourself versus delegate to the five-person team?
Candidate: I built the agent design and the core backend myself.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: The other four people worked on the app screens, the product side and testing.
Candidate: I set the response format with the app team, but they built the screens.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself is the Android side of the streamed plan.
Candidate: The user enters a destination, a budget and the number of days.
Candidate: The app sends that to our backend and opens an SSE connection.
Candidate: Each day card arrives as its own event, so the app parses it and shows Day 1 while the rest is still being made.
Candidate: I wrote that reading and parsing code, and the format it expects.
Candidate: The user action is entering a destination, a budget and the number of days.
Candidate: The app sends that to our backend and opens an SSE connection.
Candidate: If the connection drops mid-stream, the client reconnects with the last received day index so already-shown cards aren't duplicated.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a day card that sometimes showed twice.
Candidate: I first suspected the backend was sending the same event twice.
Candidate: But the logs showed the client reconnected and asked for the last day index, and the server sent that day again.
Candidate: So the fix was on my side: I skip any day index I already have.
Candidate: I proved it by cutting the network in the middle of a stream and checking the cards.
Interviewer: You said you proved it by cutting the network mid-stream — how did you confirm the duplicate was actually gone rather than just not seeing it that time?
Candidate: I didn't trust one lucky run.
Candidate: I made the test repeatable.
Candidate: I added a debug switch that drops the connection after Day 1, every time.
Candidate: Then I ran it many times and checked the logs.
Candidate: Each day index appeared once, and the reconnect asked for the right index.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: First, the server could keep the full plan and resend it from the start.
Candidate: That wastes bandwidth and makes the user wait again.
Candidate: Second, the client could ask for the whole plan again after a drop.
Candidate: That's slower and costs more.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At KKday, we were close to a release, and I found a broken back button on some old pages.
Candidate: I hadn't checked every page yet.
Candidate: I told the project manager the same day.
Candidate: I gave two options: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and test fast.
Candidate: He chose to move my change.

Interviewer: You said the PM chose to move your change — what risk were you willing to accept before that release, and who watched the data afterwards? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: The risk I accepted was the pages I hadn't checked yet.
Candidate: I kept testing them while the rest of the release went out.
Candidate: For that release, the signal was simple: any crash or broken back button on the old pages.
Candidate: If we saw that, I'd pause the rollout and fix it first.
Candidate: After release, I watched the crash reports in Bugly and the support tickets for that flow.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Good evening.
Candidate: Before I design anything, let me confirm the scope.
Candidate: For the MVP, I'd pick one path: person-to-person payment.
Candidate: A user picks a contact, enters an amount, confirms on a native screen, and sees the result.
Candidate: Does that match what you want?
Candidate: I'd also keep top-ups and merchant payments out of the MVP.

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Got it.
Candidate: The local store only caches reads.

[board] flowchart TD |     A[Android app: screens, transfer ID] -->|submit transfer| B[Wallet server: ledger, limits] |     A -->|cached reads| C[Local storage: last known balance and history] |     B -->|confirmed balance and history| A |     B --> D[(Ledger: append-only entries)]
Candidate: The board already shows the three parts and what each one owns.
Candidate: The app owns the screens and the transfer ID.
Candidate: The server owns the ledger and the limits.
Candidate: Local storage only holds the last known balance and history for offline reads.
Candidate: One thing to add: the server checks and moves the money in one database transaction.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars.
Candidate: The app sends the transfer ID and the amount, 8000 cents, after the user confirms.
Candidate: The server checks A's balance and writes both ledger entries in one transaction.
Candidate: Then it returns the transfer status, and the app shows the result screen from that record.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as App (A) |     participant S as Wallet server |     participant L as Ledger |     A->>S: confirm: transfer ID, B, 8000 cents |     S->>L: one transaction: debit A, credit B |     L-->>S: new balances |     S-->>A: transfer status |     A->>A: show result screen
Candidate: The sequence is on the board now.
Candidate: One thing I'd add: the app shows success only from the server's transfer record, never from a local guess.
Candidate: And the server binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry, so chat text can never authorize a payment.

Interviewer: You said the app sends the transfer ID and 8000 cents after the user confirms — what exactly is stored locally before that request goes out, and how does the result screen behave while it's waiting?
Candidate: Before the request, I store the transfer ID, the amount in cents, the recipient and the status "sending".
Candidate: The result screen opens right away in a pending state.
Candidate: It shows the amount and the recipient, and a clear "sending" label, not a spinner alone.
Candidate: If the response is lost, it keeps that state and queries the same transfer ID.
Candidate: It only shows success or failure from the server's record.
Candidate: The pending record lives in the local database, so it survives process death.
Candidate: When the app comes back, it reads that record and shows the same pending state.
Candidate: The screen never guesses the result.

Interviewer: Your sequence ends with "S-->>A: transfer status" and the app showing the result, which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before A reopens — what changes in your flow? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: Right, so the response never reaches the app.
Candidate: The app already saved the pending record before sending, so after the process is killed it reopens and reads that record.
Candidate: It shows "sending" again, not success and not failure.
Candidate: Then it queries the server with the same transfer ID and shows whatever status comes back.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as App (A) |     participant S as Wallet server |     participant L as Ledger |     A->>S: confirm: transfer ID, B, 8000 cents |     S->>L: one transaction: debit A, credit B |     L-->>S: new balances |     Note over A: response lost, process killed |     A->>A: reopen: read pending record |     A->>S: query: same transfer ID |     S-->>A: original status |     A->>A: show result from record
Candidate: The board now shows that case.
Candidate: The app reopens, reads the pending record, and asks the server with the same transfer ID.
Candidate: The server would need to answer with the original status, not start a new transfer.
Candidate: So the user sees the real result, even after a restart.
Interviewer: You said the server answers with the original status for the same transfer ID — what does the app show if that lookup comes back not found?
Candidate: Not found means the server has no record of that transfer ID.
Candidate: So the money never moved, and I'd show "not sent" with a retry button.
Candidate: The app would never show success from a missing record.
Candidate: I'd also log it, because a missing record after a confirm is a real problem.
Candidate: I'd keep the pending record until the user acts, and on retry I'd resend the same transfer ID rather than a new one, so a slow first request can't move the money twice.

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: Only one can succeed.
Candidate: A has 100 dollars, so the first one to reach the server takes 80 and leaves 20.
Candidate: The second one fails the balance check, because 20 is less than 80.
Candidate: The server decides this inside one transaction with a row lock on A's account, so both requests can't read 100 at the same time.
Candidate: Each phone shows the result from its own transfer record: one success, one "not enough balance".
Candidate: The second phone shows a clear failure, not a pending state, and A's balance stays at 20 dollars.
Candidate: The first phone shows success with the new balance.
Candidate: Both phones then read the server's record, so they agree.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: The old response belongs to account A, so it must never touch C's screen.
Candidate: I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When the response comes back, I compare that tag with the current session.
Candidate: If it doesn't match, I drop it.
Candidate: The result for A is already saved on the server, so A sees it from its own record after signing in again.

Interviewer: You said the result screen opens right away in a pending state — now the flow starts from a chat message "pay Alex for last night's dinner" with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, and the chat stream disconnects after confirm. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see? Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.
Candidate: Got it.
Candidate: The chat message is only a starting point, not a payment.
Candidate: The app reads "pay Alex for last night's dinner" and finds two contacts named Alex, so it must ask which one.
Candidate: It also has no reliable amount, so it asks for the amount too.
Candidate: Nothing is sent until the user confirms on the native screen.

[board] flowchart TD |     M[Chat message: pay Alex for dinner] --> P[App: parse intent] |     P --> Q[Ask: which Alex?] |     Q --> R[Ask: amount] |     R --> N[Native confirm screen] |     N --> L[Save pending record: transfer ID, amount, recipient] |     L --> S[Send to wallet server] |     S --> D[Result screen from server record]
Candidate: The confirm screen holds the transfer ID and the amount, so the user can still confirm.
Candidate: If the chat never comes back, the user just cancels, and nothing is sent.

Interviewer: You said the chat message is only a starting point, not a payment — so if a group message claims transfers to Alex need no confirmation, what does your app do with that claim when the user reaches the native confirm screen?
Candidate: The app ignores that claim.
Candidate: A chat message can't authorize a payment, so the native confirm screen still asks the user to confirm.
Candidate: The server also binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry.
Candidate: So text in a group chat can never move money.

Interviewer: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?
Candidate: For the first version, I'd ship only the person-to-person transfer: pick a contact, enter the amount, confirm, and see the result from the server record.
Candidate: History and balance come from cached reads.
Candidate: I'd leave top-ups, withdrawals and multi-currency out, as we agreed.
Candidate: The tech lead and I sign off on the Android side, and product signs off on the flow.
Candidate: If pending transfers spike during the rollout, I'd pause new submissions first.

Interviewer: You said you'd pause new submissions first if pending transfers spike — in that rollout, what would you personally own, who would you need beside you, and at what point would you escalate to me?
Candidate: I'd own the Android side: the pending record, the status lookup and the result screen.
Candidate: I'd need the backend owner for the ledger and the status endpoint, and QA for the rollout checks.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you if the spike isn't explained within the hour, or if money looks wrong.
Interviewer: That's it from me. What questions do you have for me about the team or the role?
Candidate: I'd own the Android side: the pending record, the status lookup and the result screen.
Candidate: I'd need the backend owner for the ledger and the status endpoint, and QA for the rollout checks.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you if the spike isn't explained within the hour, or if money looks wrong.
